synopsis: Space-filling designs, including Latin hypercube, Sobol and other quasi-random methods, spread continuous-parameter tests more evenly than naive random draws and are recommended for coverage, exploration and surrogate-model training [f6813, f7227, f14138]. Latin hypercube divides each parameter range into n equal slices and places n points so that every slice of every parameter is used exactly once; applications include exploring detection range under dust, glare and speed and feeding surrogate-guided search [f14136, f14144]. This geometric coverage is not probability sampling and does not represent quarry operating frequencies, where most approaches are slow and most weather is clear; it cannot establish unweighted rates or worst cases [f6815, f14140, f7229]. Unrealistic regions receive equal treatment unless constraints and distributions are added, so the booklet assigns these designs to the coverage stream alongside combinatorial designs, not as a basis for the release claim [f6816, f14143, f7353]. The stated evidence for these methods is generic expert opinion from statistical synthesis, rather than application-specific validation evidence [f7232].
